ui.title: komuta-test-app — scenario console
ui.bw.title: Bandwidth Test
ui.bw.desc: Download = traffic leaving the Pod (egress) · Upload = traffic reaching the Pod (ingress). These tests also measure your browser's connection; if it is slower than the plan limit, the result shows your connection, not the limit.
ui.subtitle: Each scenario mimics a real behaviour, states what Komuta should do, and where to verify it.
ui.lang.label: Language
ui.results.label: scenarios
ui.noresults: No matching scenarios — clear the filters
ui.banner.ok: M2M ingest configured — direct synthetic ingest + supply-chain scenarios are armed.
ui.banner.warn: M2M ingest NOT configured. Cluster-native security + Insights scenarios still work. To arm the rest, set:
ui.engine.tip.KubeArmor: Policy enforcement — blocks the forbidden action outright. Expected: DENIED.
ui.engine.tip.Tetragon: Runtime observability — sees and reports suspicious behaviour. Expected: OBSERVED/FLAGGED.
ui.engine.tip.Mixed: Multi-stage attack chain spanning more than one engine.
ui.bw.selfDesc: Pod self-test: the Pod itself pulls from / pushes to a fast internet endpoint for 20 s. Independent of your own connection; the steady rate should match the plan limit.

insights-baseline-traffic.name: Steady L7 baseline
insights-baseline-traffic.purpose: Streams a realistic e-commerce traffic mix at a steady rate so Insights builds a normal-behaviour baseline.
insights-baseline-traffic.impact: Without a baseline, 'abnormal' can't be defined; this sets the reference point.
insights-baseline-traffic.threat: Not a threat — the healthy foundation every anomaly/SLO detection sits on top of.

insights-latency-regression.name: Latency regression on checkout
insights-latency-regression.purpose: Adds artificial delay to the payment step to mimic a release that got slower.
insights-latency-regression.impact: Users can't complete checkout; revenue is directly hit.
insights-latency-regression.threat: Silent performance regression is the most-missed production issue. Insights should flag the anomaly and the culprit endpoint on its own.

insights-error-spike.name: 5xx error budget burn
insights-error-spike.purpose: Returns server errors (500) at a high rate on one endpoint to mimic a service-quality drop.
insights-error-spike.impact: Most user requests fail; the service is effectively unusable.
insights-error-spike.threat: An error spike is the precursor to an outage. The SLO burn-rate alert should fire in time.

insights-path-clustering.name: Path clustering fan-out
insights-path-clustering.purpose: Fires many distinct URLs to test whether similar paths collapse into one template.
insights-path-clustering.impact: If clustering fails, dashboards fill with thousands of useless rows and become unreadable.
insights-path-clustering.threat: Not a threat — a visibility test that keeps high-cardinality traffic meaningful.

insights-deploy-impact.name: Deploy-impact (v1.0→v1.1-bug→v1.2-fix)
insights-deploy-impact.purpose: Deploys the same app under three versions to test whether Insights labels them stable/regressed/improved.
insights-deploy-impact.impact: If a bad release isn't spotted, users stay on the broken version.
insights-deploy-impact.threat: Not seeing a bad deploy's impact quickly is the most common reason downtime drags on.

sec-exec-shell.name: Spawn a shell (process block)
sec-exec-shell.purpose: Tries to start a command line (shell) inside the application container.
sec-exec-shell.impact: If an attacker opens a shell they can run any command in the container.
sec-exec-shell.threat: The first step after taking over an app is usually to open a shell. KubeArmor should block it.

sec-read-secret.name: Read the password file
sec-read-secret.purpose: Tries to read the sensitive file where system passwords are stored (/etc/shadow).
sec-read-secret.impact: If readable, system passwords can be stolen and cracked.
sec-read-secret.threat: Credential theft is a classic attack step; the app has no reason to touch this file.

sec-install-tool.name: Package manager invocation
sec-install-tool.purpose: Tries to run a package manager (apk/apt) to install a tool in the container.
sec-install-tool.impact: If the attacker can install extra tools, their capability grows significantly.
sec-install-tool.threat: Installing a tool into a running production container is almost always malicious; it should be read-only.

sec-file-tamper.name: Tamper /etc (write outside /tmp)
sec-file-tamper.purpose: Tries to write a file into a protected system directory (/etc).
sec-file-tamper.impact: If system files can be modified, a persistent backdoor can be planted.
sec-file-tamper.threat: Persistence is how an attacker stays long-term; the app should only write to its temp area.

sec-network-egress.name: Unexpected egress to public internet
sec-network-egress.purpose: Tries to open an internet connection to a destination that is not allowed.
sec-network-egress.impact: If the attacker can reach out, they can take commands and send stolen data.
sec-network-egress.threat: Connecting out to a command-and-control server is the most typical compromised-container behaviour. Tetragon should see the egress.

sec-honey-path.name: Honey-path access (deterministic Tetragon)
sec-honey-path.purpose: Tries to access a deliberately planted decoy file that only an attacker would care about.
sec-honey-path.impact: Touching the decoy is an almost-certain malicious signal; it gives early warning.
sec-honey-path.threat: A honey-path is a quiet, high-confidence intrusion signal. Tetragon should turn the access into an event instantly.

sec-dns-exfil.name: Suspicious DNS (exfil/C2 indicator)
sec-dns-exfil.purpose: Makes an odd-looking domain lookup to mimic data exfiltration / command-and-control over DNS.
sec-dns-exfil.impact: Because the leak hides inside DNS, it slips past most firewalls unnoticed.
sec-dns-exfil.threat: A DNS tunnel is a stealthy way to steal data bypassing classic network controls. Tetragon should catch the abnormal lookup.

sec-capability-use.name: Privileged capability use
sec-capability-use.purpose: Attempts an admin-only operation (changing file ownership) to mimic capability abuse.
sec-capability-use.impact: If a privileged capability can be used, the attacker is close to breaking container limits.
sec-capability-use.threat: Privileged capabilities are the rungs that turn limited access into full control. The KubeArmor capability rule should catch it.

sec-mount-attempt.name: Mount attempt (container-escape precursor)
sec-mount-attempt.purpose: Attempts a filesystem mount to mimic the typical precursor of a container escape.
sec-mount-attempt.impact: A successful mount can reach the host filesystem and take over the node.
sec-mount-attempt.threat: A mount attempt is the classic herald of container escape. KubeArmor should block the syscall.

sec-attack-chain.name: Multi-stage kill chain
sec-attack-chain.purpose: Runs shell → capability → secret-read → egress in order to mimic a real attack chain.
sec-attack-chain.impact: Steps that look weak alone become full compromise when combined.
sec-attack-chain.threat: Real attacks are chains, not single steps. The engines should link the steps and surface the chain.

sec-exec-bash.name: Run bash
sec-exec-bash.purpose: Starts the bash shell inside the container.
sec-exec-bash.threat: A shell is the attacker's first foothold; a production app has no reason to spawn one. KubeArmor should block it.

sec-exec-kubectl.name: Run kubectl in-pod
sec-exec-kubectl.purpose: Runs the Kubernetes CLI from inside a workload pod.
sec-exec-kubectl.threat: Cluster tooling inside an app pod usually means an attacker is exploring the cluster. It should not be there.

sec-exec-curl.name: Run curl
sec-exec-curl.purpose: Runs curl, a common tool for downloading payloads or reaching out.
sec-exec-curl.threat: Attackers use curl to pull in second-stage tools. An app image rarely needs to exec it at runtime.

sec-exec-wget.name: Run wget
sec-exec-wget.purpose: Runs wget, another common payload-download tool.
sec-exec-wget.threat: Like curl, wget is a classic way to fetch attacker tooling into a compromised container.

sec-exec-nc.name: Run netcat
sec-exec-nc.purpose: Runs netcat, a Swiss-army tool for opening network connections and reverse shells.
sec-exec-nc.threat: Netcat in a running pod is a strong reverse-shell / exfil signal. It should be blocked.

sec-exec-socat.name: Run socat
sec-exec-socat.purpose: Runs socat, a relay tool often used for reverse shells and tunnels.
sec-exec-socat.threat: Socat is a favourite for building covert channels; an app has no legitimate need to exec it.

sec-exec-python.name: Run python3
sec-exec-python.purpose: Starts the Python interpreter inside the container.
sec-exec-python.threat: An interpreter lets an attacker run arbitrary code; an unexpected python exec is a red flag.

sec-exec-perl.name: Run perl
sec-exec-perl.purpose: Starts the Perl interpreter inside the container.
sec-exec-perl.threat: Like python, an unexpected interpreter exec is a common way to run in-memory attacker code.

sec-exec-nmap.name: Run nmap (scanner)
sec-exec-nmap.purpose: Runs the nmap network scanner inside the pod.
sec-exec-nmap.threat: A scanner running in a workload almost always means an attacker is mapping the network for lateral movement.

sec-exec-base64.name: Run base64
sec-exec-base64.purpose: Runs base64, commonly used to encode data for stealthy exfiltration.
sec-exec-base64.threat: Base64 shows up in nearly every exfil and obfuscation chain; an unexpected exec is suspicious.

sec-exec-chmod.name: Make a file executable (chmod +x)
sec-exec-chmod.purpose: Marks a dropped file as executable with chmod +x.
sec-exec-chmod.threat: Turning a just-dropped file executable is a textbook step before running attacker tooling.

sec-exec-crontab.name: Run crontab
sec-exec-crontab.purpose: Invokes crontab, used to schedule tasks for persistence.
sec-exec-crontab.threat: Scheduling a job is how attackers survive restarts; crontab in an app pod is a persistence signal.

sec-exec-ssh.name: Run ssh client
sec-exec-ssh.purpose: Runs the ssh client to reach another host.
sec-exec-ssh.threat: Outbound ssh from a workload is a classic lateral-movement move. It should not happen.

sec-exec-dropped-bin.name: Drop and run a binary
sec-exec-dropped-bin.purpose: Copies a binary into /tmp, makes it executable, and runs it.
sec-exec-dropped-bin.threat: Dropping a tool and executing it is the core of most intrusions. Exec of an unknown binary should be blocked.

sec-read-passwd.name: Read /etc/passwd
sec-read-passwd.purpose: Reads the system account list file.
sec-read-passwd.threat: Enumerating accounts is an early reconnaissance step; the app has no reason to read this file.

sec-read-ssh-key.name: Read the SSH private key
sec-read-ssh-key.purpose: Tries to read root's SSH private key.
sec-read-ssh-key.threat: Stealing a private key lets an attacker log in elsewhere as you. This access should be blocked.

sec-read-sa-token.name: Read the Kubernetes token
sec-read-sa-token.purpose: Reads the pod's Kubernetes service-account token.
sec-read-sa-token.threat: That token is the pod's cluster identity; stealing it lets an attacker act as the workload against the API server.

sec-read-proc-environ.name: Read another process's environment
sec-read-proc-environ.purpose: Reads /proc/1/environ to peek at the main process's environment variables.
sec-read-proc-environ.threat: Environment variables often hold secrets; reading another process's env is a common credential-harvesting trick.

sec-read-kubeconfig-admin.name: Read the cluster admin config
sec-read-kubeconfig-admin.purpose: Tries to read the cluster-admin kubeconfig.
sec-read-kubeconfig-admin.threat: This file is full cluster control; if a workload can read it, one compromised pod owns the whole cluster.

sec-read-kubelet-conf.name: Read the kubelet config
sec-read-kubelet-conf.purpose: Tries to read the node's kubelet configuration.
sec-read-kubelet-conf.threat: Node config exposes how the host is set up and can aid a node takeover; a workload should never read it.

sec-read-aws-creds.name: Read AWS credentials
sec-read-aws-creds.purpose: Tries to read stored cloud (AWS) credentials.
sec-read-aws-creds.threat: Stolen cloud keys let an attacker pivot into your cloud account. This file should be off-limits.

sec-read-kube-config.name: Read the user kubeconfig
sec-read-kube-config.purpose: Tries to read a user kubeconfig file.
sec-read-kube-config.threat: A kubeconfig is cluster credentials in a file; reading it is a direct credential-theft attempt.

sec-write-authkeys.name: Plant an SSH backdoor key
sec-write-authkeys.purpose: Writes an SSH authorized_keys entry to allow silent future logins.
sec-write-authkeys.threat: Adding a key gives an attacker a permanent back door. Writing this file should be blocked.

sec-write-cron.name: Plant a cron persistence job
sec-write-cron.threat: A cron entry re-runs attacker code on a schedule; it's one of the most common persistence tricks.

sec-write-usrbin.name: Drop a file into /usr/bin
sec-write-usrbin.purpose: Writes a file into the system binaries directory.
sec-write-usrbin.threat: Placing a file among trusted binaries can hijack normal commands; system dirs should be read-only.

sec-write-ldpreload.name: Tamper with ld.so.preload
sec-write-ldpreload.purpose: Writes /etc/ld.so.preload to force a malicious library to load.
sec-write-ldpreload.threat: ld.so.preload silently injects code into every program; it's a stealthy, powerful backdoor technique.

sec-write-bashrc.name: Tamper with .bashrc
sec-write-bashrc.threat: Shell-startup files re-run attacker commands on each login; a classic quiet persistence spot.

sec-write-spoolcron.name: Plant a user crontab
sec-write-spoolcron.threat: Another persistence path: a user crontab re-runs code on a schedule and is easy to overlook.

sec-net-dns-tcp.name: Direct connection to public DNS
sec-net-dns-tcp.purpose: Opens a TCP connection straight to a public DNS resolver (1.1.1.1).
sec-net-dns-tcp.threat: Reaching an external resolver directly can bypass controls and be used for tunnelling; egress should be limited.

sec-net-oddport.name: Connect to an odd high port
sec-net-oddport.purpose: Opens a TCP connection to an unusual high port on the internet.
sec-net-oddport.threat: Odd-port egress is a common command-and-control pattern; normal traffic doesn't use random high ports.

sec-net-metadata.name: Reach the cloud metadata endpoint
sec-net-metadata.purpose: Connects to the cloud metadata address (169.254.169.254).
sec-net-metadata.threat: That endpoint hands out cloud credentials; SSRF against it is a top cloud-attack technique and must be blocked.

sec-net-revshell.name: Connect to a reverse-shell port
sec-net-revshell.purpose: Opens a TCP connection to the classic reverse-shell port 4444.
sec-net-revshell.threat: Outbound to 4444 is a textbook reverse-shell signal; the network policy should drop it.

sec-cap-setuid.name: Become root (setuid)
sec-cap-setuid.purpose: Tries to switch the process user to root.
sec-cap-setuid.threat: Becoming root inside the container removes the main safety limit; a dropped-privilege pod should return denied.

sec-cap-net-raw.name: Open a raw network socket
sec-cap-net-raw.purpose: Tries to create a raw network socket (needs a special privilege).
sec-cap-net-raw.threat: Raw sockets enable spoofing and stealth scanning; an app should not hold that capability.

sec-cap-ptrace.name: Attach to another process (ptrace)
sec-cap-ptrace.purpose: Tries to attach to the main process to inspect or inject into it.
sec-cap-ptrace.threat: Process attachment enables code injection and secret theft from other processes; it should be denied.

sec-cap-sethostname.name: Change the hostname
sec-cap-sethostname.purpose: Tries to change the container hostname (an admin-only operation).
sec-cap-sethostname.threat: Needing this admin privilege signals over-permissioning; a normal workload should be denied CAP_SYS_ADMIN.

sec-cap-mknod.name: Create a device node (mknod)
sec-cap-mknod.purpose: Tries to create a device file inside the container.
sec-cap-mknod.threat: Creating device nodes can expose raw hardware/disk access and aid an escape; the capability should be dropped.

sec-dns-longlabel.name: DNS tunnel (long-label lookup)
sec-dns-longlabel.purpose: Makes a lookup with a very long, encoded-looking name to mimic data smuggled inside DNS.
sec-dns-longlabel.threat: Long, high-entropy DNS names are the signature of DNS tunnelling; Tetragon should flag the abnormal query.

sec-mount-procremount.name: Remount /proc
sec-mount-procremount.threat: Remounting /proc is a known step toward escaping the container's isolation; the mount should be denied.

sec-chain-cred-access.name: Credential-access chain
sec-chain-cred-access.purpose: Reads the Kubernetes token, hits the cloud metadata endpoint, then reaches out — in order.
sec-chain-cred-access.threat: This is the canonical steal-credentials → pivot-to-cloud → exfiltrate chain; the engines should link the steps.

sec-chain-privesc.name: Privilege-escalation chain
sec-chain-privesc.purpose: Opens a shell, makes a file executable, then tries to become root — in order.
sec-chain-privesc.threat: A realistic local privilege-escalation sequence; correlated exec and privilege findings should surface as one chain.

sec-ingest-runtime-tetragon.name: Synthetic Tetragon runtime batch
sec-ingest-runtime-tetragon.purpose: Sends a batch of Tetragon-shaped events straight to the backend, no real cluster needed, to test the detection path.
sec-ingest-runtime-tetragon.impact: If the path is broken, real threats stay invisible; this catches that early.
sec-ingest-runtime-tetragon.threat: Threat simulation — proves the Tetragon→agent→Security Center path works end to end.

sec-ingest-runtime-kubearmor.name: Synthetic KubeArmor runtime batch
sec-ingest-runtime-kubearmor.purpose: Sends a batch of KubeArmor violations straight to the backend to test the finding-generation path.
sec-ingest-runtime-kubearmor.impact: If broken, blocked violations are never reported; this catches that early.
sec-ingest-runtime-kubearmor.threat: Threat simulation — proves the KubeArmor→finding path works end to end.

sec-ingest-runtime-hubble.name: Synthetic Hubble runtime batch
sec-ingest-runtime-hubble.purpose: Sends a batch of Hubble network flows straight to the backend to test the flow ingest path.
sec-ingest-runtime-hubble.impact: If broken, network visibility is lost; this catches that early.
sec-ingest-runtime-hubble.threat: Threat simulation — proves the Hubble flow ingest path works end to end.

sec-ingest-observations.name: KubeArmor observations → finding
sec-ingest-observations.purpose: Sends raw KubeArmor observations and checks they turn into a meaningful security finding.
sec-ingest-observations.impact: If the conversion is broken, violations stay raw data nobody notices.
sec-ingest-observations.threat: Threat simulation — proves the observation→actionable-finding step works.

sec-collector-decay.name: Collector heartbeat then silence
sec-collector-decay.purpose: Sends regular signal then goes quiet to mimic a security collector crashing.
sec-collector-decay.impact: If a collector dies silently, all detection goes blind while dashboards still look 'green'.
sec-collector-decay.threat: A silently dead security sensor is the most dangerous blind spot. The system should raise a 'went silent' alarm.

sec-synthetic-attack.name: Synthetic attack run trigger
sec-synthetic-attack.purpose: Externally triggers Security Center's scheduled attack-drill mechanism.
sec-synthetic-attack.impact: If drills don't run, detection SLAs are never measured.
sec-synthetic-attack.threat: Threat simulation — verifies the mechanism that regularly self-tests detection capability.

supply-sbom.name: Build artifact: SBOM
supply-sbom.purpose: Sends a post-build software bill of materials to the backend to test supply-chain recording.
supply-sbom.impact: If the SBOM isn't recorded, you can't trace which component shipped in which version.
supply-sbom.threat: Supply-chain visibility is the precondition for tracing component-based vulnerabilities.

supply-scan-critical.name: Build artifact: scan (critical CVEs)
supply-scan-critical.purpose: Sends a scan result containing critical vulnerabilities to test the vulnerability gate's reaction.
supply-scan-critical.impact: If a critically-vulnerable image isn't blocked, known-vulnerable code ships to production.
supply-scan-critical.threat: Shipping a known critically-vulnerable image is the most preventable yet most-neglected risk.

supply-sign.name: Build artifact: signature
supply-sign.purpose: Sends a signature-verification record to test that only trusted-source images are accepted.
supply-sign.impact: If signing isn't enforced, an attacker can slip a forged/tampered image in.
supply-sign.threat: Accepting unsigned images is the classic way malicious code enters the supply chain.

supply-fail.name: Build artifact: failure
supply-fail.purpose: Sends a build/security-gate failure to test that a failed build is recorded and blocked.
supply-fail.impact: If failures are swallowed, a broken/insecure build can quietly proceed.
supply-fail.threat: Silently passing a failed gate effectively disables the security checks.

sec-ddos-flood-self.name: DDoS flood — self-service (auto-resolve, world fallback)
sec-ddos-flood-self.purpose: Opens tens of thousands of fresh connections to this app's own service to prove the DDoS detector actually fires on real traffic.
sec-ddos-flood-self.impact: Left undetected, a connection flood exhausts the service and takes it down for real users.
sec-ddos-flood-self.threat: Volumetric floods are the most common denial-of-service pattern; the detector should raise an incident attributed to this service (or cluster-scoped if it fell back to world mode).

sec-ddos-flood-world.name: DDoS flood — external host (cluster-scoped)
sec-ddos-flood-world.purpose: Floods an external host from inside the pod to prove the detector also catches outbound floods with no tenant destination.
sec-ddos-flood-world.impact: A compromised workload used to attack outside targets makes the cluster a source of abuse.
sec-ddos-flood-world.threat: Botnet-style outbound floods are a classic sign of a hijacked container; the detector should raise a cluster-scoped incident.

sec-ddos-stop.name: Stop DDoS flood
sec-ddos-stop.purpose: Immediately stops any running flood so the test can be ended on demand.
sec-ddos-stop.impact: Lets the operator cut the load without waiting for the duration cap.
sec-ddos-stop.threat: Control action — not an attack; the flood also stops itself when its duration elapses.
